title: Gadget Review: LiberNovo Omni - the USB-C powered office chair ★★★★⯪
content:
Whenever a company asks me to review their gadgets, I always ask if it is USB-C powered. If not, I'm not interested. So, welcome to the future where your chair is USC-C rechargeable!

WHAT?!

The LiberNovo Omni looks like a standard office chair - but has two secret features.

First, is that it is exceedingly comfortable. Full foam cushions, lovely headrest, and a recline which almost gets you horizontal.

Second, it is USB-C powered. There's a small battery pack which plugs in to the chair. Why? Read on!

OK, let's start at the beginning.

Assembly

Flat-pack chairs like this are normally notoriously hard to assemble. The LiberNovo bucks that trend - not only does it include a how-to video, it prints the instructions on a MASSIVE piece of cardboard.

I'm used to peering at tiny black-and-white diagrams in a flimsy paper booklet. IKEA could learn a thing or two from this.

The screws are all labelled and a hex-driver is included. What's an even nicer touch, however, is some safety gloves:

That's the sort of thing which doesn't cost much to the manufacturer, but is such a thoughtful gesture. There's nothing too sharp as you assemble, but who wants to cover their new chair in blood, eh?

The parts come in two large boxes, but there aren't that many separate bits.

Building it took about half an hour. It's easier with a friend to help - as are most things in life - but doesn't require much skill.

Go Back To The USB-C Part Again Please?

The battery pack is a 2200mAh unit with a USB-C port to recharge. It connects in to the chair with this slightly unusual connector:

The internals of the chair have a USB-C cable to connect everything up.

LOL!

YES BUT WHY DOES A CHAIR NEED A BATTERY PACK??!?!

On the side of the left arm-rest are three buttons.

Two of them move the lumbar-support up and down. Depending on how your back is feeling and how far you are reclined, you can adjust the the back-support position.

And the 3rd button?

That's the build-in back massager, silly!

Is that useful?

Yes. Being able to instantly adjust the back support without having to twist around is fantastic, especially for those of us reaching a certain age.

The "massage" feature essentially just moves the support up and down for five minutes before returning to its previous location. When sat upright, it feels great. But the real benefit is when you're laying down.

How flat does this thing go?

160° - not quite flat, but good enough when you're taking a break from Typing Real Hard. You don't want a photo of me sprawled out, so LiberNovo have helpfully provided some stock photos of much better looking folk.

It is incredibly stable. At no point did it tip over or feel like it was going to deposit me on the floor. What really helps is the included foot stall.

No Feets On Seats

Unsurprisingly, this is not USB-C powered. A sturdy plastic footrest with a deeply padded leg rest on top.

Again, assembly was a cinch - follow the large printed instructions and clip it together. It's rated for 40㎏, so you shouldn't stand on it but it is more than enough to rest your weary legs.

Price

I hope you're sitting down for this.

Direct from LiberNovo, you can expect to pay around £700 - although there are bundles with extra batteries, the footrest, and even an eye mask which will shoot that price up. You can get the full bundle on Amazon for around £1,000.

There's two ways to look at that price. Firstly, youch. But, alternatively, that's still cheaper than a Herman Miller Aeron. And Herm's doesn't come with a built-in lumbar massage.

(There is also an upgraded version which has a built in fan under the seat. Personally, I suggest eating a healthier diet.)

I can't deny that's a chunk of change. If you're anything like me, you probably spend most of your day sat down. You might as well sit on something comfortable.

Final Thoughts

Having the back-rest adjustable via arm-rest buttons is a genius touch. I just wish it went further. I'd love a control panel (or, dare I say it, app) which let me adjust the seat height, recline, headrest position etc. Who can be bothered with fiddly manual levers when electricity can do the work for us?

Building this chair was a breeze - and it was delightful to get a pair of safety gloves with it.

The chair is extraordinarily comfortable and the back massage, while not on the level of a "shiatsu" style heated massage pillow, is delightfully pleasant. Would I lie all the way back and sleep in it? Yeah! Certainly more comfortable than an economy airline seat.

If you spend a lot of time sitting at your computer, your arse deserves something supportive. Your back deserves some love too. Yes, the USB-C power-pack is a little bit of a gimmick - but it is a hell of a good one.

In my opinion, this is worth splashing out on.

title: Poles and polars
content:
The previous two posts have been about polar triangles. The first used a polar triangle to derive a theorem, and the second showed how to compute polars using linear algebra. But what exactly is a polar triangle and why is it called that?

Poles and polars on a sphere

Let’s start with a sphere S and a great circle G. Then G is the intersection of S with a plane through the center of S. The circle G has two poles, two points on opposite sides of S that are as far as possible (i.e. π/2 radians) from G. If you rotate the sphere so that G is the equator, the poles are the north and south pole.

Conversely, if you start with a point P on the sphere S, the polar of P is the great circle for which P is a pole. So if you think of P as the north pole, the polar of P is the equator. The term equator would have been more intuitive than polar, but the terminology was established a couple centuries ago.

In my opinion it would be clearer to call poles and polars both duals. The dual of a great circle is a point, and the dual of a point is a great circle.

Now let’s look at a spherical triangle ABC sides a, b, and c. The vertices of the polar triangle of ABC are the poles of the sides a, b, and c. This definition is essentially correct, but it needs a little refinement.

The pole A′ of the side a is one of the two poles of the great circle containing a, the one that that lies in the same hemisphere as A. Define B′ and C′ similarly, and the polar triangle is the spherical triangle with vertices A′B′C′.

Poles and polars in the plane

The terms pole and polar were coined for spherical geometry, then generalized to plane (projective) geometry. If you think of great circles as the lines of spherical geometry, then you can carry the idea of poles and polars over to plane geometry where the pole (dual) of a line is a point, and the polar (dual) of a point is a line.

However, in the plane you can’t define the pole of a line without more context. You have to start with a circle (or more generally a conic section) and define the pole of a line with respect to the circle and the define the polar of a point with respect to the same circle.

Given a circle S with center O, to find the polar of a point P ≠ O, let Q be the inversion of P in S, and let ℓ be the line through Q perpendicular to the line OP.

Conversely, the pole of a line ℓ with respect to a circle S is the inversion of Q in S where Q is the intersection of ℓ with OQ. Here we assume the line ℓ does not pass through the center of the circle O because otherwise O = Q and it doesn’t make sense to speak of the line OQ.

Projective geometry

The definitions above have a couple holes that can be filled in by extending the Euclidean plane to the projective plane.

We defined the pole of a line ℓ except when ℓ passes through the center of the circle. If ℓ passes through O then the pole of ℓ is the point at infinity in the direction of ℓ. Similarly, we defined the polar of all points except O. In projective geometry, we can define the polar of O to the be line at infinity, the line containing all the points at infinity.

The post Poles and polars first appeared on John D. Cook.

title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
content:
Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months. All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok.

June 26, 2026

OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna. Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50, while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10. They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it.

June 30, 2026

Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed. Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up.

July 24, 2026

Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol). Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed.

July 30, 2026

OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02.

August 10, 2026

Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent.

August 21, 2026

OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ($4 / $20 / $0.40) for the next three months.

September 1, 2026

Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25, which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1, cut the cache read cost by 75%.

Cache read costs

When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn. Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider). Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote!

September 3, 2026

OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost. Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable.

September 22, 2026

OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol! They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ($0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01) of the previous version.

On the same exact day, Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”. Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post).

September 29, 2026

It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ($2 / $10 / $0.10) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper.

Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago. These price cuts also apply to model usage from subscription agentic harnesses such as Codex and Claude Code. More importantly, these models do not appear to have cut any corners in terms of output quality to achieve their price cuts.

From the timeline above, there is a clear tit-for-tat between Anthropic and OpenAI, and it is reasonable to assume that these particular price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic are in reaction to each other. However, no one cuts prices by 80% unless there is some externality in play. So, what gives?

The Behavioral Economics of LLMs and Competitor Pricing Pressure

If you have been testing agents with new LLMs as they are released, it can be very difficult to differentiate them outside of subjective vibes. Since last November that launched the hypergrowth of agentic LLMs, models have become more of a commodity where it’s trivial to try a new model on your codebase with just a toggle in a harness like OpenCode and Zed Agent, or a different API endpoint string through OpenRouter, and as a result there is little moat. Additionally, there are many competitors—not just large companies like Google and Meta—who can provide models which are sufficient substitutes and therefore allow pricing pressure.

For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1, which also recently released an updated 1017 variant.

The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time. That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised. I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models. Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise (45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003. Note the operative words “from DeepSeek”.

On OpenRouter, any inference provider can list a model that they host, and when a user hits the OpenRouter API, the request is routed to one of those models—it’s routed to any available model by default for load balancing but the developer can specify preferences such as “lowest price” in the API request. Back in May, I noted that there were 13 distinct providers hosting DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter. For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers.

However, looking at the effective input costs (which account for the interaction between cache read costs and cache hit rates), many distinct providers are close costwise.

OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D. Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs. Opus 5.5 at 58) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ($2 / $10 / $0.20). It’s the same size and architecture as Kimi K3 which is currently being hosted by over 20 distinct inference providers: once the weights drop on November 4th, you can therefore expect most of them to support the new Kimi K3.1 Pro model at a roughly equivalent price. Notably, Moonshot AI itself is joining the price cut fun and priced Kimi K3.1 Pro at less than the original Kimi K3 ($3 / $15 / $0.30).

One recurring trend among vocal AI detractors is that the price of tokens has been kept artificially low to hook people into the LLM ecosystem, but then the prices will increase to “the true cost of a token” and the AI boosters will be screwed once the free ride ends. The theory is that OpenAI and Anthropic are loss-leading just like what Uber and Lyft did to the ridesharing industry in the 2010s, but unlike then, OpenAI and Anthropic are not a duopoly who have the sole power to set prices in the ecosystem and the barrier to entry for the inference industry is not as high. As long as these many inference providers can continue to serve models at a similar price and a similar quality to what OpenAI and Anthropic can provide, and switching cost is negligible, then the prices may continue to decrease more. It’s no surprise both companies are trying to build moats to defend against this trend, such as a focus on enterprise commitments and personal agentic assistants like OpenAI Dots and Claude Duet.

The idea that token prices will suddenly rise is more a fantasy that is not supported by both behavioral economics and the actual trends of LLM prices going down significantly over the last few months for better models, and not just from OpenAI and Anthropic. As long as scalers can price at a cost-per-token lower than the revenue-per-token, then those inference providers will reduce token costs to compete with each other to a point that OpenAI/Anthropic will have to lower their prices to compete too. The 29 distinct providers on OpenRouter have little incentive to serve an unprofitable model (they would just stop serving it and use the compute capacity for a profitable model instead) and “the true cost of a token” may end up being where price equals marginal cost.

On that note, both OpenAI and Anthropic are indeed close to IPOing, which raises further questions about the price cuts.

IPO Pumping

The timing of these price cuts is notable because both OpenAI and Anthropic are rumored to be IPOing soon—OpenAI in 2027, and Anthropic within a couple months. So far, leaked financials from both OpenAI and Anthropic show unsurprisingly that they are losing billions due to R&D/scaling, albeit in both cases these reports do not account for the hyperexpansion of agentic LLM use over the past few months. Investors will scrutinize the massive negative profits and demand that they have a plan to turn things back around.

So, why did they cut their primary revenue source by up to 80%? That’s the opposite of what you would want to do to look good on an S-1 prospectus! The profit margins on inference themselves likely tell a different story, with some reports saying the profit-per-token margins are as healthy as 80% with caveats. How much of a profit margin do they have after these major cuts?

Speaking personally, the price cuts have indeed affected how I spend on LLM agents, but not in the way I expect OpenAI/Anthropic want their typical customer to behave. I used to have a $100/month subscription to Codex (the 5x Pro plan) when GPT-5.6 Sol was the top model, and I managed to just fully exhaust all the usage included in the subscription despite getting annoyed with random usage resets. Once GPT-6.1 Sol released and I noticed that the cost of using it was effectively cut by 75%, you know what I did?

I cut the max usage quota to 1/5th after getting 4x more efficient usage of the same model, so it ends up roughly neutral and the obvious choice.

In fairness, the profit margins for subscriptions such as Claude Code and Codex are uncertain given their immense value relative to the API usage, and if there are capital crunches I suspect subscription value will be cut before the base price of the models. For example, at the same time GPT-6.1 Sol was announced, OpenAI cut the usage allowance by 50% for the $200/month tier in Codex under the argument “to reflect our increasingly efficient models”—which is technically correct but it’s funny to put in writing.

I will be very curious to see the Anthropic IPO prospectus and the inference profit margins once it becomes public soon.

I also question whether it’s good for OpenAI/Anthropic if they intentionally obsolete their more expensive models. After Opus 5.5 released a month ago, there hasn’t been any discussion about either Fable 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra because Opus 5.5 is just that good.

I fully expect a Fable 5.2/GPT-6.1 Astra to release in a couple weeks and prove me wrong, and I will be very curious to see how it will be priced.

Another less-cynical factor that could explain the price cuts is that LLM infrastructure has improved over the past few months—when Anthropic said “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that,” I believe it. One outcome that would be genuinely ironic is that if these models are more compute efficient, it reduces the need for these massive data center buildouts, which could cause cascading economic failures. However, that likely won’t happen since inference is only one part of the compute mix and those data centers are still needed for other parts of the pipeline.

Overall, the price cut is weird, but as a user I’m certainly not complaining! Open-weight models and secondary inference providers will continue to serve as an economic check on the prices of LLMs and other business shenanigans the large labs may concoct. Even if Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs are catastrophic and cause both companies to fold, it will not suddenly cause LLMs and agents as an industry to die.
description: What is “the true cost of a token”?

title: A rising tide raises all rents
content:
Imagine, for a second, that AI really does become too cheap to meter. What happens next?

I've heard hype that says there'll be a productivity boom to rival the internet, electricity, and spinning loom. That ideas and skill and taste will become the new currency, that 5 people can do the work of 500. Maybe. I think this is directionally correct but a bit exaggerated.

But here's a more interesting question: Who benefits from that productivity?

If software is no longer scarce, what still is? Where are the bottlenecks? How does that shape the world, and what emergent behaviors result?

I posit that it partly goes to the people building, partly goes to incumbents, mostly goes to landlords and other rent-seekers, and hardly any of it goes to everyone else.

To avoid that situation, we need an equivalent of Land-Value-Tax that works for scarce resources other than land. I propose some potential approaches towards the end of this post.

Possible worlds

Consider five different scenarios.

Status quo

In our baseline, AI doesn't do anything useful, or it works but it doesn't do that much. Maybe it has about as much impact on the world as the invention of the mobile phone; culture changes around it, but the world is fundamentally the same place. Let's call this a "status quo world". I personally think the status quo is quite unlikely, but maybe you feel differently. If so, and you hate AI, you can stop reading right here, the rest of the post will just make you mad.

Messy transition

For this and all future worlds, let's assume AI really does work and really does result in greatly increased productivity that revolutionizes the economy. Not only that, but also that we get at least a limited form of "recursive self-improvement" where improvements in AI get faster as AI itself gets better. 1 What next?

Will AI take our jobs? We're already seeing this to some extent in markets that are "AI-exposed", such as programmers, translators, and people just entering the job market. But that doesn't necessarily mean they can't get other jobs. The National Bureau of Economic Research published a paper about exactly this possibility in 2019:

[…] the displacement effect of automation has been counterbalanced by technologies that create new tasks in which labor has a comparative advantage. Such new tasks generate not only a positive productivity effect, but also a reinstatement effect—they reinstate labor into a broader range of tasks and thus change the task content of production in favor of labor. The reinstatement effect is the polar opposite of the displacement effect and directly increases the labor share as well as labor demand.

History is also replete with examples of the creation of new tasks and the reinstatement effect […]

In this world, there are a lot fewer programmers, but a lot more UI designers, sales engineers, and HCI researchers. There is significant short- and mid-term displacement, but in 10 years things shake out mostly ok. Labor has less influence over capital than today; wealth inequality gets worse; careers and jobs become more unstable. Overall though, people can still make rent 2. Let's call this a "messy transition world".

Reinstatement failure

What happens if the reinstatement effect fails? What if jobs change faster than people can retrain, and long-term employment becomes more and more unstable? What if nearly all jobs become automated?

Well, first we're going to see labor lose out power against capital. As this spreads to other industries and demographics, we'll start seeing more and more unemployment. People and organizations who were lucky enough to catch the automation wave start accumulating more and more wealth; an ever-narrowing fraction goes to people who work for a living. Eventually, a small plutocracy controls the majority of the world's wealth.

This is possible on an economic level, but also on a geopolitical level. Not every country has its own GPU foundries; not every country is part of the global supply chain for those foundries. We could see a post-modern version of colonialism, mediated through markets rather than force.

This plutocratic world is not stable. It's the nature of plutocrats to try and accumulate more and more power, and to automate more and more of the labor that generates their income. Unlike today, they will actually have the power to do so, and unemployment spreads like wildfire. An increasing portion of the population is simply unable to find a job.

If this gets bad enough, I see one of three possible political reactions, in the sense of an action taken by a country's government.

Stable equilibria

Butlerian Jihad

If a government takes no action at all in response to increasing unemployment, people get more and more desperate until there is violent revolution. One possibility is that the revolution is crushed, and the country becomes a North Korea-like autocracy (hopefully we can all agree this is bad). Another possibility is that the revolution succeeds.

Now, I have friends who think that Revolution Is The Answer, and will usher in the Fully-Automated Post-Scarcity Luxury Gay Space Communism of the future. I, unfortunately, am not so hopeful. Looking at history, and at small-scale upheavals in my own communities, I just don't think this is going to happen. You have to remember: someone who's been unemployed for years due to AI is angry. They're not going to care whether you were using AI to build solar panels, to automate driving a truck, or to build military drones; they're just going to see someone who has contributed to their helplessness.

Instead, I think revolution would look more like Frank Herbert's Butlerian Jihad, or Walter Miller's A Canticle for Leibowitz: Indiscriminate destruction; mass pogroms; loss of human knowledge; book burnings. It's much easier to destroy things than to rebuild them.

Revolution is not inherently liberatory! If it doesn't completely destroy the institutions that maintain our society, the most likely outcome is "the same as always, with someone else in charge". Even Robespierre was in favor of property rights. At a bare minimum you need a plan for self-correcting systems that react to changing events.

Bread and circuses

A government could react earlier. The most likely reaction I foresee is to extend existing welfare and unemployment programs, in effect resulting in Universal Basic Income (UBI).

This is good! I am in favor of UBI! However, UBI does not guarantee a good life for the people receiving it. Eliezer Yudkowsky, as much as I hate to give it to him, has a good article about this called Universal Basic Income and Poverty:

it only takes a life lacking in one resource needed to survive, to produce some quality that I think ancient poor people would also recognize as 'poverty'.

It's the quality of working yourself until you can't work any longer; of taking on jobs that are painful to do, and require groveling submission to bosses, because that's what it takes to get the few scraps to hang on.

[…] somehow there is a Poverty Equilibrium which beat a 100-fold increase in productivity plus everything else that went right over the last thousand years. […]

I do not understand the Poverty Equilibrium. So I expect that a Universal Basic Income would fail to eliminate poverty, for reasons I don't fully understand.

I think what Yud is missing here is very simple: rent-seeking and incumbent effects. A world where everyone has, say, a guaranteed minimum of 50k annual income, is a world where rental housing costs about 25k a year and the rest goes to food, utilities, transport and healthcare. Above a certain point, making food/utilities/transport/healthcare cheaper doesn't help in the long term, because it just results in housing swallowing an ever-increasing proportion of income.

Don't just take my word for it. Henry George, Enrico Moretti, and Richard Hornbeck all predict near-total capture of productivity increases by landlords and economic rent-collectors when housing supply is sufficiently limited. Their findings are pretty bleak!

This world is explored further in "Manna", a fictional dystopia where all service jobs are automated down to the minute by an AI "manager" that whispers tasks into everyone's ear. The end result is a permanent underclass, half of whom work precarious jobs with extreme hours, and the other half of whom are permanently unemployed and live in government-sponsored housing.

Let's call this a "rentier world", for the plutocracy that makes their money through rent and capital, not through innovation. Here, people can rent enough to survive, but scarcity is everywhere, and almost no one owns anything that would give them power.

Distributed ownership

"Manna" explores another world, one where automation improvements are captured by the whole population, not just plutocrats. Scarcity is, essentially, a thing of the past. There is no real-estate mogul extracting rent, because there is no land ownership. There is no one working themselves to death, because everyone has plenty. Instead, the land and production are split equally between everyone in the society.

Now, I think Manna has a lot of funny ideas (constant surveillance sounds a lot like a dystopia to me), but its ownership model is quite interesting. The catch, of course, is that we have to get there somehow.

Let's call this a "post-scarcity world", for the abundance that's present throughout the society. This is the world I want to see. This is the world I want to build together.

Distributing ownership

How do we build a post-scarcity world? How do we distribute the enormous amount of material wealth in our society to everyone within it?

Tax rents, not capital

In economics, there is a concept called deadweight loss. Most taxes are "inefficient" in a broad sense. For example, when you tax food, you cause people to buy less food or cheaper food, with negative health outcomes. This inefficiency is called "deadweight loss". A tax is "efficient" if it does not introduce deadweight loss.

Lars Doucet, writing on Scott Alexander's blog, talks about Georgism and Land Value Tax:

George argues that poverty paradoxically advances alongside progress because, as material conditions improve, landowners can charge more rent for locational benefits they didn’t create. […]

Henry George’s remedy is the land value tax, or LVT. In its ideal form, this tax would capture and redistribute the annual rental value of land; that is, the recurring value of the land excluding the value of any buildings or other improvements on top of it. In practice, this looks a lot like a conventional property tax paired with a “universal building exemption.” Notably, George isn’t simply in favor of a land value tax; he’s also opposed to taxes on both labor and capital.

[…earlier…] Keep in mind also that the Georgist Land Value Tax is pair [sic] with a "Citizen's Dividend" or what we see as UBI, so that it's not the government claiming land rent, rather the land rent is taxed and split up equally for all men.

Land-value tax is efficient! I said above that UBI doesn't help much because demand-side interventions just raise housing costs. Conversely, LVT does help because the supply of land is fixed: landlords are already charging as much as their tenants can afford, so when taxes go up, landlords have no choice but to pay the tax out of pocket.

Not only that, but I think this is conceptually the right model: There's a difference between a landlord who owns the property and does nothing to work on it and a property-management company who's responsible for fixing issues. The property-management company is doing useful work; the landlord is not. We should pay people for the work they've done (improvements built on land, and maintenance of those improvements), while not allowing them to capture value from the underlying shared resource (the land itself).

Measuring value

So how do we figure out the value of land?

LVT is generally measured using appraisals which distinguish "improvement value" from "land value". You get the latter by looking at prices for properties with little improvement (parking lots, empty fields, etc.) and then comparing that to the price of buildings in nearby areas 3.

We said earlier that LVT works because the supply of land is fixed. There are other areas where supply is fixed: radio broadcast spectrums, IPv4 addresses, mineral and resource rights, utility contracts.

Land and IP addresses are in some ways the hard cases because they're private property. For public property, like radio spectrums and resource rights, there's a much simpler solution, which is to force an auction for ownership of the right every so often. If the incumbent wins, the auction acts as a tax; otherwise, the incoming owner pays the tax. Either way, the owner pays fair market value. The US government already auctions off spectrum rights.

Note that this is auctioning the right to the scarce resource, not the capital used to develop that resource. For example, a radio broadcast company retains their broadcast towers if they lose an auction; they only lose the spectrum itself.

Tax cash flow, not income

Another term in economics is economic rent. This refers to income that is not necessary to incentivize valuable work or investment. In other words, the "rentier" is collecting more income than justified (in the sense of "economically worthwhile") by their risk + investment + labor. This often happens when the rentier controls a scarce good that no one else is able to create or buy.

Not all rentiers are landlords 4. I know someone who ran a "Managed Service Provider". This is a kind of IT company where a business pays a fixed fee every quarter, in exchange for having all their computer problems repaired at no additional charge. This particular company was a registered "Authorized Service Provider" for a large computer manufacturer, which means that the MSP was authorized to conduct repairs on behalf of the manufacturer without voiding the hardware warranty. This is quite relatively rare; most companies do not have this relationship.

The owner sold most of the company many years ago, but kept one thing, which was the repair authorization. They no longer do any work for the MSP at all, but employ a project manager, who takes contracts, delegates them to subcontractors, and coordinates between them and the manufacturer. The owner takes some profit off the resulting fixes after paying the contractors and project manager. This is also a form of economic rent: The owner's income comes from controlling access to the authorization, not from labor, risk 5, or investment.

How do we distinguish the rent extracted by this MSP from the valuable production? With LVT, we can value the land separately from the improvements built on top, but here the authorization is inextricably tied to the work being done in its name. We want to share the rents that the MSP receives, without discouraging the real positive impact it has by fixing computers.

One possible solution is to not try to separate these in the first place. Cash flow tax is a generalization of LVT to other kinds of resources, keeping the same idea of taxing rents and deducting investments. The UK's Institute for Fiscal Studies has published a paper on exactly this:

The intuition is that the company is taxed immediately on all receipts but can immediately deduct all outgoings at the same rate: with a 25% tax rate, the government covers 25% of the investment cost and takes 25% of the return, essentially becoming a compulsory silent partner in the project. If the revenue is worth more than the cost, 75% of the revenue will be worth more than 75% of the cost, so any project that is worthwhile before tax will be worthwhile after tax 6. That is a good thing.

"Any project that is worthwhile before tax will be worthwhile after tax" is another way of saying this is an efficient tax that causes no deadweight loss. 7 "Compulsory silent partner" means that every citizen of the country is invested in every company, indirectly through the government. This applies to companies that fail, not just companies that succeed! Under this scheme, a company that loses money receives a tax refund, not just a tax deduction. Just like LVT would be the only tax on property, this would be the only tax on corporate profits, replacing existing taxes. Norway already does something like this for oil and hydropower.

We would apply deductions and refunds to wages, not just to capital investment. The government would pay a portion of every salary and independent contract, at the same rate as the rest of the cash-flow tax. This avoids incentivizing investment over labor.

Why is this better than a corporate profit tax? Precisely because the refunds and deductions avoid deadweight loss. Because it causes no economic distortion, we can raise the tax much higher without disincentivizing useful work. If we take our earlier MSP as an example, they would pay more tax on their profits, but much less in wages, because the government helps them cover that cost.

Distribute the funds

Using our tax income, we would redistribute it to everyone in our society as dividends. This would be unconditional, without means-testing. Our LVT and cash-flow taxes give everyone an economic stake in productivity improvements, which means the money doesn't immediately evaporate into economic rent and corporate conglomerates 8. People still spend their income on housing, but most of the money goes back into the dividend pool through LVT. Similarly, money spent on goods and services goes back into the pool, tying dividends to the whole economy rather than to the minimum necessary to live.

This is not new. Both Alaska and Norway both discovered enormous reserves of oil and put the profits into reserves that are saved and redistributed for the benefit of all citizens. It really is politically feasible to make these changes when there's sufficient wealth floating around.

With these funds, people would become much much less dependent on their employer for a stable source of income. This is good, because as AI and automation develops, there will be fewer jobs. By themselves, dividends don't give us post-scarcity, nor independence from work. What they do give us is a way to ensure that benefits to a small segment of the population are shared between everyone. If, in the future, we have enough productivity and resources to support everyone on dividends alone, we have the governance processes in place to make sure we end up in a post-scarcity world rather than a rentier world.

This doesn't work automatically. The taxes have to be high enough that the dividends make up for lost work hours during the transition period. We'd need some way to avoid companies from simply relocating to somewhere with lower taxes. But—if we somehow manage that—I really do think we'd have a bright future ahead of us.

Transition plans

If you call your representative to ask them to increase taxes on landlords; homeowners; conglomerates; and banks; and then redistribute the money to everyone as dividends, they will laugh you out of the room. These are some of the most powerful and influential groups in politics, in large part due to their giant rental incomes. Just saying "hi could you dismantle the political machine please" will not work. Instead, we need some sort of incremental transition that appeases existing interests.

Homeowners

Let's start with homeowners. The traditional problem here is people on fixed-income who cannot tolerate tax increases. If you switch from property taxes to LVT, and this results in a net tax increase, they really do experience material hardship.

One possible solution is to defer the increased tax until after the sale of the property, charging interest on the deferral. Until then, the tax collected stays at previous values, avoiding a sudden "spike" in costs for people on fixed income. This still results in an overall wealth transfer, just delayed by a few years; and because it's tied to the sale, you're not punishing people for ownership: selling gives them the free cash they need to pay the tax. This would be a one-time deferment; unlike California's Prop 13, it would go away after the first sale.

Note that we want new houses to be built, we want them to sell at market price. What we don't want is for people's life savings to be tied up in their home, and for landlords to make a giant profit even when they're not doing any maintenance. I do not believe that home ownership is intrinsically good.

Businesses

Businesses have a clear motivation here: our cash-flow tax gives them a discount for all investments. Even raising the tax is not necessarily bad for the business, because it gives them more cash up-front, allowing them to take more risks and start more projects. The strongest opposition would be from businesses who make few investments but collect a lot of profit, i.e. exactly the people we want to redistribute wealth away from.

If government budgets are a problem, we could "ease in" the tax over time for new projects, keeping current profit tax rates and adding investment deductions until the two rates match. Only then would we raise the overall cash-flow tax rate.

Conclusion

The goal of this proposal is not to take away profits from people who are earning 'too much', or to single out landlords as uniquely bad. The goal is to give everyone a stake in productivity improvements in a way that still keeps the natural self-regulation of the free market, and to make people economically secure without being dependent on their employer. I want to live in Asimov's, Iain M. Bank's, Kim Stanley Robinson's post-scarcity worlds. And I really do believe that we have a path to get there. We just need to open our eyes and walk down it.

In other words: Land is different from capital. Economic rent is a curse. Economic security is freedom.

To all a good night.

Bibliography

  • “Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence”, Brynjolfsson et al.
  • “Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor”, Acemoglu and Restrepo
  • “Robots, Growth, and Inequality”, Berg et al.
  • “Karl Marx”, Ben Macready
  • “The Culture”, Culture Wiki
  • “Butlerian Jihad”, Dune Wiki
  • “A Canticle for Leibowitz”, Wikipedia
  • “Sur la propriété. Projet de déclaration des droits de l’homme et du citoyen”, Maximilien de Robespierre
  • “Project Cybersyn”, Wikipedia
  • “Universal Basic Income and Poverty”, Eliezer Yudkowsky
  • “Progress and Poverty”, Henry George
  • “Local Labor Markets”, Enrico Moretti
  • “Estimating who benefits from productivity growth”, Hornbeck and Moretti
  • “Manna – Two Views of Humanity’s Future – Chapter 1”, Marshall Brain
  • “Manna – Two Views of Humanity’s Future – Chapter 5”, Marshall Brain
  • “Deadweight loss”, Wikipedia
  • “Does Georgism Work? Five Years Later”, Lars Doucet
  • “Your Book Review: Progress And Poverty”, Lars Doucet
  • “Welfare Economics of the Land Value Tax”, @BlueRepublik
  • “Land Valuation: Direct Land Capitalization (The Income Approach to Value)”, California State Board of Equalization
  • “About Auctions”, United States Federal Communications Commission
  • “Economic rent”, Wikipedia
  • “Managed services”, Wikipedia
  • “Authorized service provider - Wikipedia”
  • “Original equipment manufacturer - Wikipedia”
  • “Full expensing and the corporation tax base: Green Budget 2023”, Adam and Miller
  • “Taxes 2025 For the 2025 Budget Year: Tax on resource rent industries”, Norway Ministry of Finance
  • “Our History”, Alaska Permanent Fund Corporation
  • “The fund”, Norges Bank Investment Management
  • “Deferral of Local Property Tax (LPT) payment”, Irish Tax and Customs
  • “1978 California Proposition 13”, Wikipedia
  • “The 30-year Mortgage is an Intrinsically Toxic Product”, Byrne Hobart
  • “Moore’s Law for Everything”, Sam Altman

  1. I am explicitly not considering a "singularity" or "FOOM"-type situation. I don't think it's possible to make any useful predictions about singularity, and furthermore I don't think singularity is very plausible in the first place. ↩

  2. I try very hard to distinguish "housing costs" from "economic rent" in this article, but in this one place I've blurred it because I don't know a better common phrase for it. I mean housing costs specifically. ↩

  3. it's a lot more complicated than this in practice, but this is a reasonable mental model. ↩

  4. And landlords are not purely rentiers; they do some amount of work in the form of repairs and upkeep. ↩

  5. They do accept some amount of risk, but not any more than their administrator does. ↩

  6. In many countries, this would mean an investment can be "double-deducted": first the investment itself gets a tax deduction, then the interest repayment gets a deduction. In some cases this can result in the government losing money while the company gains. This can be avoided by simply removing the deduction on the interest payment. ↩

  7. Within a country. It can still incentivize companies to change their headquarters to another country. ↩

  8. Sam Altman, of all people, wrote about this in 2021. ↩
description: If AI restructures the economy, who benefits?

title: lighting the skies
content:
Someone stated in the early days of the war, a feeling that was reciprocated by the soldier in khaki and the sailor in blue, that a mechanical device would be the determining factor in ending the world conflict, favorably, of course, for the United States and her allies. 1

One of my common topics is the history of nuclear weapons. The "atom bomb" is a rich vein of history because its impact has been as much cultural as technical. Dramatic depictions like Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer have recently enforced, perhaps even revived, the perception of nuclear weapons as an innovation that forever changed warfare. More quietly, historians and strategists tend to wonder if that is still true today, or if it was ever as true as was supposed—the conventional firebombing of Tokyo probably claimed as many victims as the nuclear attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, for example. Besides, it's not unusual to hear people overstate the significance of nuclear weapons to WWII in a way that is obvious with a brief inspection of the timeline. The technology became available only very late in the war, and for that reason if no other, it must have had less of an impact on the outcome than other revolutionary wartime developments like radar.

Why is it that radar, a complex technology that fundamentally changed the landscape of aerial combat, seems so pedestrian? Perhaps because the technology has far more non-military applications, and so is more familiar to our everyday lives. Perhaps because the development of radar was scattered between countries and institutions without the involvement of such intriguing figureheads as J. Robert Oppenheimer (although one wonders if this is because we have not looked as close; certainly radar figures like Henry Tizard had colorful lives as well). Perhaps because radar just isn't as exciting: it does not put on anything like the show of a nuclear detonation.

Today, we consider another such step in military technology. This is an invention that forever changed the battlefield, and it's one that does put on a show. In fact, that has become the technology's main purpose. From the 1870 siege of Paris to the modern used car lot, searchlights have marked many of history's great conflicts—and great deals.

The concept of electric light has been known since the very early 19th century. An electric arc lamp, or at least one of their ancestors, was demonstrated in 1806. Because of the widely known story of Thomas Edison's incandescent lamp, most people know that electric light had a very difficult journey from idea to practical device. That path was not as simple as what we are taught in schools: besides the several other inventors with a good claim to the lightbulb, incandescent lights were just one of a few technologies that developed in parallel.

Before controlled incandescence, the principal form of electric light was still an arc. Arc lamps also did not fall to incandescent bulbs as quickly as you might think. Arc lamps remained the preferred choice for very bright, high-CRI lighting into the mid-20th century, and reached what will likely remain their ultimate form in the late 1960s, as the 15 kW Xenon arc lamps used by IMAX projectors. Along the way, arc lamps displaced many of the early forms of artificial lights: Oxy-hydrogen candles, known as "limelights," fell out of theatrical use. "Moonlight towers" began the displacement of gas lights for street lighting.

And the military—the military readily adopted this new form of reliable, practical, powerful lighting.

Calling In Light

The effect of artificial lighting on military tactics could fill a book. I will focus on one narrow part of this story, but it will be helpful to set the stage with a few of the earlier developments. For much of the pre-electricity era of military history, artificial lighting was mostly a disadvantage. Fires, torches, and other practical sources of light were bright enough to reveal one's location but not bright enough to search anyone else out. Ironically, the main interest that military researchers had in light was often to suppress or conceal it.

The chemical light technology developed for theaters and displays had promise, though. One of the first recorded uses of a powerful light for a military venture (and, as far as I can tell, the very first recorded use of a searchlight) came in the context of the American Civil War. The Union Navy sought to economically attack the Confederacy by maintaining a persistent blockade on southern ports; the Confederacy sought to maintain trade, often by sending out "blockade runners" under cover of night. A Union ship, perhaps frustrated by firing aimlessly into the dark, improvised: a theatrical light was mounted to a crude reflector, forming the first naval searchlight. It wasn't a very good one, it was dim and unfocused and the sailors struggled even to keep it lit under maritime conditions. It was good enough, though. By first following the sound, and then casting the light, the Union ship was able to engage the Confederate vessel even on a moonless night. Amusingly, while this incident is widely described in histories of military signals and lights, I have found none that state the outcome. Perhaps it was unfavorable to the victors.

Electric arc lamps were far more suitable to military use: simpler to operate (although not as simple as we might today expect), more flexible in their placement, and by the end of the Civil War brighter. The 1870 Siege of Paris, part of the Franco-Prussian War, was a bellwether in the history of military aviation. Cut off on the ground, the French made extensive use of balloons (a technology they had pioneered in the 18th century) to move people and mail. In the process, several records for aerial travel were set. The French enjoyed air superiority and had little need for air defense, but the situation on the ground was much more troublesome. Prussian forces mounted lengthy artillery bombardments, causing devastation limited mostly by the range of their cannons. For the soldiers manning Paris's fortifications, it was important not only to keep attackers outside of the city, but to keep them as far away as possible.

Paris, not for nothing known as the "City of Light," had seen demonstrations of arc lamps back to 1850. The invention of the arc regulator (which advanced the carbon rods to keep the arc intact) and improved batteries made the lights more practical by 1870, and during the early days of the siege "electricians" were hastily recruited to the city's defense. They manned a variety of arc lamps installed around the city, limiting the cover of darkness for nighttime assaults. At the summit of Montmartre hill, a position with a clear view over one of the most vulnerable parts of the city's defense, they installed one of the most impressive lights ever built. Not only was it larger than the others, it could operate for longer: the power supply was not a battery, but a dynamo powered by a steam engine. Besides that leap into modern design, the Montmartre light also presents an early example of "tipping and cueing" in intelligence gathering. French intelligence agents, having caught wind of a surprise attack, sent a message to Montmartre where the light's skilled operators aimed it by heading and elevation before applying power to catch the enemy in quite a compromising position.

A decade later, the military searchlight had become a standard technology. The Royal Navy regularly equipped ships with dynamo-powered, carbon-arc searchlights starting around 1882. They found that, besides their role in aiming weapons, searchlights could be something of a weapon on their own. Aiming searchlights back at coast defense artillery positions not only exposed them to incoming fire, it also dazzled the gunners and frustrated their efforts to accurately aim at the ships. This principle was memorably demonstrated by a 1903 US joint maneuver exercise, in which the Navy's Atlantic Fleet mounted a simulated attack on Long Island Sound. All together, on cue, the ships trained their searchlights on the main defensive battery at Fort Michie. The soldiers at the fort didn't manage a single shot, they were so blinded by the lights—and limited in their ability to even move around the battlements, since they could so plainly be seen (and fired upon).

As the military developed searchlights, they were quickly applied to civilian use. Limited availability of electricity, and limited need for such powerful lighting, meant that searchlights wouldn't yet become part of the urban landscape. They were reserved for special events, especially those with an emphasis on technical demonstrations. Of course, such events were bounteous around the turn of the century in the form of various world fairs and expositions. Perhaps the first use of searchlights as a device for entertainment came at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, which was extensively lit by electricity. A total of 17,000 horsepower of steam engines (so, yes, presumably steam horsepower, a curiously different unit from the one we are familiar with today) powered thousands of arc lights.

Most of these were for illuminating the fairgrounds and its many monuments, but some were installed for the sake of light itself. On the roof of the Liberal Arts Building, a searchlight claimed to be the most powerful yet made could light a newspaper well enough to comfortably read at a distance of eight miles. Of course, it was more than just a book light—it was a way to attract attention. Unlike the military context, civilian searchlights were deployed specifically to be seen. Rooftop searchlights became a common feature of large expositions, and by lazily searching the sky they established an atmosphere while guiding curious onlookers to the site of the event.

Even this early, it was known that searchlights could be a powerful form of advertising. At the Chicago World's Fair, the upstart Cloud Projector Company demonstrated a searchlight with a lens system that could focus a slide onto the cloud layer. It was literally a cloud projector, in the modern sense, and giant words floating ethereally in the sky announced the fair's upcoming special events.

In 1901, the Pan-American Exposition was underway at Niagara. Among the attractions was a demonstration of electrical arcs produced by a 40 kV transformer recently installed at the Niagara Falls power station. Alongside that light show, a second, more controlled form of arc was displayed: searchlights. These were described as an application of military technology, and specifically of military signaling technology. Searchlights were installed atop the "Electric Tower" at the exposition grounds, and at a viewing tower erected at Niagara Falls proper. At night, the two lights—22 miles apart—were each plainly visible from the other tower. The military was, of course, well aware of this potential use and as soon as searchlights had been installed on Navy ships they came into use as a means of communication.

Extensive newspaper coverage of the Exposition means that we know more details of these machines. The searchlights used for the tower demonstrations had 30" reflectors, and consumed 80 amps at about 50 volts for 4 kW give or take. This was indeed a very bright light for the time, and at the Exposition, the searchlights were swung around among various targets. "As the beams of the projectors sweep across country," The Virginian-Pilot wrote, "the residents of the villages and country places will enjoy the illumination." Excitement for the lights was such that newspapers throughout the region published Morse code tables, in the hope that anyone in the region could decipher news bulletins that were sent from the signal lights.

Watching the Skies

Electric light is far from the only invention to make a dual appeal to spectacle and the military. From the Wrights' first controlled flight in 1903, it only took about seven years for the Navy to envision the aircraft carrier. The 1911 Italo-Turkish war featured armed biplanes, and as the hostilities of the First World War opened the US Army flew airplanes into Mexico, in pursuit of Pancho Villa. In 1915, the Austro-Hungarian Aviation Troops bombarded the Serbian city of Kragujevac from biplanes. Serbian soldiers fired on them with small arms, but had no success. A private, though, got a lucky shot with an artillery gun. This was the first instance of ground-air combat, and the first use of air defense.

By the latter part of WWI, aircraft were in routine use as both bombers and fighters. One tended to lead to the other: our 1915 takedown notwithstanding, bombers and reconnaissance planes enjoyed almost complete freedom of the skies in the first few years of the war, until Germany's fighters presented meaningful resistance. Ground-based air defense lagged behind, but in an interesting turn of aviation history, the held-over use of tethered balloons as observation posts provided a key motivation for improved anti-air artillery. These balloons were conspicuous and almost defenseless, so ground-based escorts accompanied them.

Balloons—and in the case of the Germans, Zeppelins—remained an important part of WWI air units. Besides their ability to hang around for an extended period of time, airships could carry much larger payloads than early bombers. Zeppelins occasionally loomed over London, raining down the era's most sophisticated destruction, from 1915 to 1917. These lumbering vessels had their vulnerabilities, though. Big, slow, and flammable, they were easy to take out with artillery fire if you could spot them. German air raids were conducted at night, and by the end of the war Zeppelins were being painted a non-reflective black.

By 1916, a network of 258 searchlights across England hunted the skies for airships. There were as many anti-aircraft guns, using the pencil-beams of the searchlights as aiming guides. Air defense was so new at the time that little military doctrine had developed around it, and Britain's first searchlight units were found in the Royal Engineers. As in France, the searchlight operators were known as electricians, specifically the Electrical Engineers.

These units had actually formed prior to the outbreak of WWI, for the purpose of coastal defense. None other than Chief Scout Lieutenant-General Robert Stephenson Smyth Baden-Powell (yes, the 1st Baron Baden-Powell) had improvised the use of a chemical searchlight to keep ships away from a besieged town during the Second Boer War; the Electrical Engineers had relieved the use of chemical lights in South Africa when they arrived with arc lights. By 1914, the Electrical Engineers had six companies in London as part of the Territorial Army. With the outbreak of the World War they were immediately put into service, as were other Anti-Aircraft Searchlight companies across Britain. Soon, other companies were deployed closer to the front in Europe.

1910s carbon arc search lamps were not always easy to operate. Most military searchlights by that time were built on the back of trucks, with combustion engine dynamos as a power supply. A typical WWI searchlight unit had three lights, five trucks, and 28 soldiers. Searchlight units became a natural home for other air defense technologies then under development, so that by the end of the war some units had acoustic reflectors (for detecting aircraft by sound) as well.

One of the lessons learned during the First World War was that searchlights were quite flexible. Portable searchlights could be used for air-defense, or could be positioned on a hill to light the battlefield (and even dazzle attackers). A technique called "artificial moonlight" took advantage of the enormous output of carbon arc lamps by pointing a searchlight up at clouds and letting the clouds reflect the light back to earth. This dim illumination could help an infantry unit move at night; commanders had the moon on demand.

On the other hand, searchlights were vulnerable. Experiments in mounting searchlights on airships to light the ground were of limited success, the lights made the position of the airship obvious and it would quickly be shot down. Similarly, as air-ground combat techniques evolved, searchlights became the first target for incoming enemy aircraft. Destroying the searchlights meant that anti-air guns were firing blind.

Even after the First World War established searchlights as a defensive technology—their sweeping beams portending destruction—the public didn't lose its affection for a bright display. In an apparent homage to the use of arc lamps for both stage plays and film projectors, Hollywood's Egyptian Theater had searchlights atop its facade from its opening day. Perhaps inspired by the 1895 installation of an ex-Chicago World's Fair searchlight in Pasadena, the Egyptian Theater's lights announced premieres by sweeping the sky—promotional searchlights learned from air defense, and ironically, the post-WWI fashion for major events was to aim lights upwards, rather than downwards at terrain as had predominated before the war.

Grauman extended the concept to his other theaters, with both permanent and portable lights often used at the Chinese Theater. In 1930, for the opening of Howard Hughes's "Hell's Angels," 200 searchlights lined Hollywood Boulevard. The scene could have easily been mistaken for a major air raid, but instead it became part of Hollywood culture. Three years later, 20th Century Pictures adopted its memorable emblem, surrounded by beams of light.

Hollywood's searchlights spread beyond just theaters. In 1931, Fisher Motors De Soto-Plymouth on Hollywood Boulevard opened under sweeping lights. Auto dealerships always wanted attention, and searchlights were the perfect combination of electrical modernity, show business spectacle, and mystery.

Synchro Searchlights

Searchlight technology advanced incrementally between the First and Second World Wars. Carbon-arc lamps remained the underlying technology, but features like automatic carbon regulators (that "fed" the carbon rods towards the arc as they burned away) and foot switches for easy control became standard. A common searchlight at the beginning of WWII might range from 8 to 24 kW, and by the end of the war the largest units reached over 100 kW.

The greater innovation of that war was the integration of searchlights into electromechanical fire control systems. New electrical technology, specifically a clever device called a "synchro" or "selsyn," revolutionized searchlight units. A synchro is a way of electrically transmitting a position. Two devices, similar to AC motors, are coupled by a three-phase circuit such that rotating one will rotate the other in proportion. The two "ends" of the synchro will always have the same relative position, so that by putting a synchro transmitter in one place and a synchro receiver in another, you can remote control the position of a device like a searchlight.

Synchros were immediately applied to "distant electric control," still a common term in marine searchlights. One of the main problems with the searchlight has always been its tendency to attract enemy fire. Early searchlights often had two operators sitting on chairs to the back or side, cranking wheels for azimuth and elevation. These two operators were often killed early in the engagement. By the use of distant electric control, a searchlight's operators could hide some distance from the searchlight or even operate it from a fortified position like a bunker. This turned out to be a superior way of using a searchlight anyway: operators directly beside later searchlights were practically blinded by the light reflected back by dust and vapor in the air. An operator some distance to the side had a much easier time seeing what was at the end of the beam.

Many US air defense searchlights offered a backup, as well: a control crank at the end of a metal arm, called an extended hand control. Were the electrical control system to fail, a searchlight operator could at least stand ten or so feet off to the side and be that much further from incoming fire. Practical use of searchlights for air defense by WWII required adaptation to the better ground-attack capability of aircraft. Searchlights might be stored in a concrete bunker and rolled out on tracks for use, by soldiers who would quickly retreat from the searchlight to a hidden control point. If the searchlight was struck, the operators at least survived, and a well-equipped unit would have a second light ready to go. The purpose of the concrete searchlight shelters was mostly to ensure that a "spare" searchlight would survive the shrapnel from an attack on the one in use.

The synchro could also integrate searchlights with other air defense equipment. Early in WWII, radar had not yet been fielded, and acoustic locators remained the state of the art. But they were now part of a unified system: two operators on a set of acoustic listening horns would spin cranks to adjust horizontal and vertical position until the sound of an airplane's engines was loudest. By synchros, this position was transferred to a searchlight control station. These stations resembled a large pair of binoculars on a sort of articulated mount. The base of the control station had readouts for the azimuth and elevation from the acoustic locator, and the operator started by turning wheels to aim the remote searchlight where the locator indicated an aircraft should be present.

Once the aircraft was caught in the beam, the searchlight operator threw a transfer switch that placed the searchlight under control of the synchros in the articulations of the binocular mount. From this point on, they tracked the aircraft through the binoculars, and the searchlight followed automatically. The azimuth and elevation from the binoculars could be sent by yet other synchros to readouts at an anti-air control station or even directly to a firing computer that aimed guns.

All of this required adjusting for the different locations of each of these components. A combination of old fashioned fire control techniques (placing each station along a common base line) and analog computers did that trick, already well-established technologies since similar computations were needed to aim guns in consideration of gravity and wind.

Speaking of a common baseline, it is also worthwhile to discuss the use of searchlights in coast defense during WWII. For a period of the war, the US feared a naval attack, particularly on the West Coast. Similar systems were widely deployed for firing artillery at attacking ships. A set of observation stations, placed along a common baseline, took azimuth readings to enemy ships. Those readings were reported by messenger, and later transmitted by synchros, to a plotting room where a mechanical and later analog computer determined the position of the ship. Yet other computers, at fire control points, determined how to aim the guns.

Because this whole system relied on baseline stations visually spotting ships through theodolites, it was much less effective at night. Searchlights were added to many installations, remote controlled by synchros from the baseline stations. Like the azimuth-indicating spotting scopes, two searchlights trained on a ship from a well-surveyed baseline gave enough information to compute a firing solution.

Advancing technology obsoleted the whimsical acoustic locating horns. Infrared heat detectors, looking much like searchlights but operating more or less in reverse, were the first electronic means of detecting aircraft in the night. They soon gave way to the first radar sets. The SCR-268, introduced in 1940, was the US Army's first fielded radar system. Its huge beam antenna had three operators on a bench hanging from the back, spinning cranks to adjust the antenna position until oscilloscopes showed the strongest possible return. The SCR-268 was a drop-in replacement for the acoustic locators in searchlight units, but it was far more effective. Skilled radar operators could place an aircraft accurately enough that it was centered in the searchlight beam before the light was turned on. Besides giving enemy pilots quite a surprise, this gave them little time to evade or return fire before anti-aircraft guns were zeroed in from the searchlight.

The British developed a more refined version of the SCR-268 called the Searchlight Control Radar. It is notable for its far more compact design, small enough that its antennas were mounted directly to the searchlight under control. The result is almost cyberpunk, a 1.5 meter light bristling with antennas, operators hanging from the sides. The SLC is said to have raised the chances of spotting an inbound aircraft with the searchlight from 1% to 90%.

Consider a typical World War II searchlight, the GE Model 1942, introduced the year that its model number suggests. This 60" searchlight came on a trailer, with a second trailer up to 600 feet away for the 12 kW diesel power plant and the control station up to 300 feet away. What we might now call accessory interfaces allowed the searchlight to receive synchro signals from a locator and send them to a firing computer. These searchlights still required quite a bit of maintenance, and they provided features to ease that work, like a work light inside the searchlight drum for replacing the carbon rods.

The Second World War also brought about a renaissance in aerial searchlights. Mostly abandoned in the First World War because of their tendency to attract fire, searchlights returned to aircraft for a decidedly nautical use. Submarines, all diesel-electric during WWII, typically surfaced at night to run their engines and charge their batteries. The first submarine-hunting aircraft used compact carbon arc searchlights to pick submarines out of the dark. The system was remarkably effective, and prompted a change in strategy for diesel submarines, which had to rely on their own anti-aircraft weapons rather than mere stealth.

Radar complemented the searchlight, but only for a short time. Radar locators for searchlights were basically an interim measure, making the best use of early radar sets that were sensitive enough to detect aircraft but lacked the spatial resolution to locate them precisely. Radar engineers, especially in Britain, made rapid improvements. For anti-submarine warfare, for example, shortwave radar systems were far more sensitive. It wasn't long before radar could directly guide anti-aircraft weapons, as well.

Military searchlights had a role to play all the way through the Korean War, but a much reduced one. Anti-aircraft detection and firing is now firmly the domain of electronic warfare: radio waves, not light beams, search our skies.

Surplus Light

The declining relevance of searchlights to the military proved an enormous boon to their civilian use. Searchlights were tremendously expensive, so promotional use had been limited to major events like world's fairs. During the war, on the other hand, the Army had built thousands of them. Afterwards, through the War Surplus Administration, it parted with most of them at bargain rates.

Entrepreneurial spirits, many of them veterans of the war, purchased secondhand air defense searchlights and offered them for advertising. Just about any auto dealership could afford to hire a searchlight for a sale, and many did. In California, it became traditional for dealerships to bring in searchlights to announce the new model year.

There is a bit of moth in every human being, operators of giant searchlights have found. Whenever a searchlight is probing into the night sky, motorists are apt to go blocks, even miles out of their way to track down the source. [^2]

Growing up in Portland, I remember seeing strange lights in the sky and searching for their origin. The searchlights utterly fascinated me, even if the source inevitably turned out to be another car lot. In New Mexico, promotional searchlights are rare, although not unheard of. The predominant weather may be a factor, since cloud cover makes searchlights more obvious. But it's mostly a matter of geography: the largest concentration of military searchlights was on the West Coast, and many overseas units were returned to West Coast ports. Los Angeles became the capital of the searchlight because they were cheapest there.

There are still WWII military surplus searchlights in promotional use, but far fewer than there once were. Parts are hard to come by, and the operation of carbon arc lamps is a less familiar skill. Most of these searchlights are eighty years old, and built to designs that would have been familiar one hundred years ago. Because of radar's dominance, the military has little need for such powerful lights and no longer buys them in quantity. Promotional searchlights have once again detached themselves from air defense, developing as a separate industry.

Modern searchlights use Xenon lamps, similar to carbon arcs in their use of an electrical arc as the light source, but far more refined. The arc is confined in an environment of Xenon gas, which practically eliminates electrode wear. Companies like Luminator make several-kW Xenon searchlights that can be mounted to aircraft, the main remaining use of searchlights for tactical purposes. Promotional systems have become much more specialized: Sky Tracker makes a popular system that mounts four 2 kW or 4 kW Xenon searchlights in the bed of a pickup truck. The four lights are attached to a common cam that rotates them in a "clover leaf" pattern, quite nonsensical for the historic application of air defense. Nonetheless, that clover leaf or vortex pattern is probably what most people now think of when searchlights are mentioned.

Fixed searchlights, of the type that graced so many World's Fairs, are now rare. The most famous in the US, if not the world, is the Luxor Sky Beam in Las Vegas. Often said to be the brightest light in the world, the tip of the Luxor pyramid contains 39 7 kW Xenon searchlights for a total of over a quarter of a megawatt, all fixed straight upwards. Even that light may be in its twilight years: since 2008, it has operated at only half power.

Today, concerns of light pollution, impact on aviation, and a general sense that auto dealerships should not lay claim to the sky have led to a decline in searchlight advertising. We are perhaps fortunate that the Cloud Projector Company's plans for on-cloud advertising didn't pan out; our present advertising industry is dystopian enough. Still, I am but a moth, or at least I have the impulses of one. There's nothing quite like a searchlight.
